children: Twilio's Chief Operating Officer Thomas Wyatt on the company's reset, why the agentic era is an accelerant rather than a threat, and where India sits in a five-lever growth plan

Most people have used Twilio without ever knowing it. When a bank asks a customer to prove who they are before letting them into an account, or a courier pings a message to say a parcel is minutes away, the plumbing underneath is frequently Twilio's. That is the company's pitch in a sentence, i.e., it is the infrastructure layer beneath the ordinary, unglamorous business of a brand talking to a consumer.

"Twilio is much of the infrastructure under the hood that makes all that happen," says Thomas Wyatt, the company's Chief Operating Officer. "Our software technology is embedded in many of the consumer applications people use day in and day out. It just allows for programmable software-powered voice, text, and email to all happen without the complexity of a brand having to build it all themselves."

The company was founded in 2008 in San Francisco, California, by founders Jeff Lawson, Evan Cooke, and John Wolthuis. The company went through a change in guard in 2024, which led to the appointment of Khozema Shipchandler as the new CEO. As of Q2 2026, the company has reported a revenue of USD 1.5 billion (a record quarter, up 22 per cent.)

The channel mix is actually wider than most assume. Voice and messaging account for the largest share of traffic and transactions, email is a substantial third, and over-the-top channels sit alongside them, with WhatsApp dominant in particular geographies. Wyatt insists the channels themselves are not the product. "The real value of Twilio isn't the individual channels themselves.

It is the ability to sign in with the Twilio platform and program your messages, deliver your conversations across a variety of channels. It is really up to the consumer to participate in or engage whatever channel they prefer. And as a brand, you just want to be able to reach them across any of them", he added.

That business rests on a dense web of relationships Twilio does not own. Carriers and telecom operators sit on one side; over-the-top platforms such as Meta's WhatsApp, RCS providers, cloud providers and email providers on the other, each with its own commercial terms and its own regulatory baggage. Increasingly, voice model providers are part of the same picture.

On the customer side, the footprint runs from self-serve developers who sign up online to large enterprises, including Reliance in India, one of the company's biggest accounts. A channel partner ecosystem extends its reach into markets where Twilio has no boots on the ground. Its recent acquisition activity, most notably of agent security firm Stitch, has been pointed squarely at identity and fraud.

Speaking on the sidelines of the company's forum in Singapore, following a keynote and a run of live product demonstrations, Wyatt walked through the reset that reshaped Twilio, the agentic shift he believes plays to its strengths, and the guardrails he thinks the industry still owes itself.
The Reset That Stuck
Twilio spent 2024 in an uncomfortable spotlight, with an activist investor on the register and a
growth-at-any-cost
model under scrutiny. When asked what exactly survived that period and still shapes the company's direction, Wyatt frames it as a return to first principles rather than a retreat.

"The company was going through a bit of a transformation and part of that pivot was, it was a high-growth company with a high spend as well to go along with it," he says. "We have become much more fundamentally sound from a financial perspective, and part of that has been really looking at what is the core competency of what Twilio does well, and that is providing communications infrastructure."

The company had been climbing up the stack, away from infrastructure and towards applications. Customers, he says, told them otherwise. “We realised that our customers really valued more of us being an infrastructure provider, and that allowed us to be a bit more focused. As part of that, we were able to drive more innovation in our platform to create more synergies between the various infrastructure services we provide. That led to accelerating growth, and at the same time allowed us to be more efficient with the way we spend our capital, which allowed us to improve profitability”, Wyatt adds.

The turnaround over the past two years, he argues, is a second-order effect of that narrowing. "It's largely powered by the value we drive for customers. Just simplifying what we offer and integrating it better has helped us tremendously."
Building For Machines, Not Just Humans
If there was one takeaway from the day's sessions, it was that the next era belongs to agents. Wyatt's view is that Twilio's infrastructure was never exclusively for people in the first place.

"We fundamentally believe the communication infrastructure that we're providing is not just for the human; it's actually for the AI agent itself as well," he says. The distinction matters at the level of design. Historically, customers embedded Twilio's functionality into a mobile app or a web workflow, and a human clicked through a sequence of steps. "Over time, agents begin to do that on a human's behalf. And agents don't necessarily interact with a website the same way a human would."

That has pushed Twilio to build what Wyatt describes as a specific agentic framework, so its capabilities can be invoked by software rather than navigated by a person. "We've embedded a lot of our core APIs into the connectors that agents or agent builders use when they build agents, whether it's the traditional AI building platforms like the large language models, or it could be through an MCP server, which is effectively the connector between Twilio and these large language models."

The intent, he says, is to remove the engineering tax altogether. "We're really building the tool set that our brands that use Twilio, they don't have to necessarily learn how to codify all this. We're giving them the tool set and the templates to be able to do that via agents."
Buy, Build Or Partner
Twilio's stack has thickened considerably over the years through acquisition, from its customer data platform through to security and identity assets. Is M&A now the company's innovation engine?

Wyatt pushes back on the framing, without disowning the strategy. "We were primarily a build company, fundamentally. The majority of our products have been organically built. The majority of our revenue is that way as well. But we are surgical about using M&A largely for accelerating roadmap."

The pattern, he says, is small technology and talent deals in markets Twilio has already decided it should be in. Stitch is the template: an acquisition anchored around agent security, agent identity and device fingerprinting, capabilities he calls essential for the modern era. "I think you'll continue to see us be aggressive in M&A when it comes to accelerating our roadmap. But the majority of our growth is coming from the organic development of the product, the platform itself, and better go-to-market execution as well."
Anything on the horizon? "We're always going to be looking and having conversations," he says. "Nothing I can share and announce today."
Neutral By Design

India has produced a crop of credible voice AI companies, and the obvious question is whether Twilio intends to work with any of them. Wyatt does not name names, but he does set out a clear rule of engagement.

"Our fundamental partner strategy is that we want to be interoperable with as many partners as we can. There are very specialised providers in different countries, as you mentioned, that we would want to be able to integrate with."

In practice, that means two delivery models. Some customers want something turnkey. "We'll plug in a partner of choice that we are comfortable using, and that might work well for some customers." Others want control. "Others might say, hey, listen, I want to pick and bring my own voice foundational model into your platform. Can I just connect it? Absolutely, you can."

The underlying position, he says, has not changed. "Twilio's philosophy has always been flexibility and being neutral in terms of our technology choices, to give customers the ability to bring their own stack, and that includes the voice functionality as well."
Five Levers, And Where India Fits
Wyatt organises Twilio's growth strategy around five levers, and the first two, he says, matter disproportionately in Asia Pacific and Japan.

The first is the self-serve, digital online business, which is how most customers meet Twilio at all. "They come to Twilio, and they get started with one or two use cases, and then it expands, and we have a direct sales motion, a global team including here at APJ, that specialises in helping customers go from that initial land to a much longer, deeper relationship and expand with us. And that business is growing really fast in APJ and continues to be the anchor of a lot of our new customer development."

The second is direct regional investment. "We pick core countries, and we focus on verticalised use cases within those countries, and we try to make sure that we can offer differentiated product integrations and capabilities with the ecosystem around those particular countries." The result, he says, is that "APJ has been growing either at or above the company average for many quarters now."

The third is the partner ecosystem, which does the work Twilio's own headcount cannot. "Twilio doesn't necessarily have people on the ground in every country, in every region, in the same way we would like to. Partners are a great way to expand our reach. They bring a lot of localised expertise. In some cases, our customers work more closely with their partners than they do with Twilio."

The fourth is cross-sell and upsell, and this is where Wyatt's argument about infrastructure versus channels comes full circle. "The real value isn't providing customers with a voice service or a messaging service. It's the integration of those services with software capabilities that sit on top of them, that allow you to orchestrate a set of messages across a variety of channels relative to a long-term conversation with the customer.

It's understanding the context of what's personal about this person you're interacting with and retaining that memory over time, and connecting that with real-time voice analytics, for example, which allow you to understand sentiment in the time of a conversation between a customer and a brand."

On India specifically, he sounds enthusiastic; however, he did stay quite on numbers. Twilio does not break out investment by country, though he confirms the spend spans research and development, customer care and the go-to-market build. There is also a reverse flow he thinks is underappreciated, i.e., Indian companies buying Twilio to serve customers outside India. “We don't disclose investment by country”, he said. "But certainly it is an area where you can imagine Twilio has a pretty big footprint in the region."

He points to Reliance Retail, one of the companies that was there on event day in Singapore, as both a marquee account and a teacher. "We've learned a lot about the region by working with them, because of the complexity and the scale that they deal with. They're using a lot of our core data platform services to build more customised audiences and journeys for so many of their different use cases."

The honest assessment on market share is that there is a long way to go. "The key there is understanding what the local needs of Indian consumers. How do you reach them at that scale? What are the types of regulatory issues you've got to work through? It's a market that we're early in our penetration of, but it's very important in terms of how we think about it."
The Moat: The Dependency Is The Barrier

Wyatt has said publicly that Twilio is no longer an API company but an infrastructure one. Pressed on the fact that much of that infrastructure belongs to somebody else, namely the world's telecom operators, he argues that the dependency is precisely the barrier to entry.

"There's so much complexity when it comes to the regulatory and compliance environments globally and then the telecommunication network," he says. “But that's not just the telcos. It's a lot of over the top, it's the Meta, it's the WhatsApp, the cloud, the RCS are a different service provider. And then you've got voice and you've got email, which is again a different type of service provider. When we think about infrastructure, we're talking about abstracting the complexity of all of that so our customers don't have to worry about it”, he added.

Which leads to his sharpest line of the conversation, and the one that frames AI as a tailwind rather than a threat. "AI is actually an accelerant for Twilio, largely because customers that are building AI agents need to exercise the infrastructure that we provide. You can't code your way into doing what Twilio does. It's all of that core relationship development, carrier agreements, the regulatory understanding, the compliance, the fraud operations that come with it. That is a relatively key part of our overall moat."
Guardrails, And Who Should Set Them

With governments, industry leaders and AI labs arguing publicly about whether the pace of AI development should be slowed, Wyatt's answer is characteristically operational. He is less interested in the philosophical debate than in the plumbing of control.

"Our philosophy has been, from the beginning, that agents require really strict controls in terms of identity verification, what they have access to, being able to do that for how long, and then providing an audit trail of exactly what they've done."

That is the strategic logic behind Stitch, which he says bolsters Twilio's one-time password, two-factor authentication and fraud risk engine capabilities for a world in which the entity logging in may not be a person. "We can help our customers detect early on when an agent is trying to log into a service.

Number one, is this agent authorised to do so, and for how long, and how are we going to audit that? And number two, there are also risk score assessments based on both human and agent logins, and our ability to provide back, through an API, a risk assessment, a score saying, hey, this is a person or an agent that should be authorised to use your service or not, and block it."

On the wider question of whether the frontier itself should be slowed, he declines to arbitrate. "We're investing heavily in helping contribute to what the industry is trying to do, to put some guardrails around this. But we're not obviously in the day-to-day research of what the labs are doing specifically when it comes to the governance process for releasing new models. I think that's an open question, but we're certainly happy to play our role in that."
What Comes Next?
Asked what excites him most about the future, Wyatt returns to convergence, and to an argument about what intelligence actually requires.

"We talked a lot about AI today being a general intelligence that horizontally understands a lot," he says. "But unless it is connected directly to the memory of who the person is engaging with it, it isn't all that intelligent at all."

That, in his telling, is the whole thesis. "Twilio is shifting from being an API company that is providing a very simple set of use cases for a specific purpose, to becoming more of an infrastructure service provider that you can exercise a lot of functionality on. We think that elevates our relationship with our customers, because we become a more strategic partner to them."

Additionally, the customer base, he expects, will soon include a great many entities that are not human at all. "It is not just for human use cases; it is for AI agent use cases as well, and because we have always been designed for builders, from the ground up, we think we are well-positioned there to continue to have success in the agent era."
